(1) A nonempty ℛ s \mathcal{R}_{s} warrants Act with an action from that set; the shared action need not be unique. If every admissible case is feasible but the intersection is empty, Ask-Preference or Ask-Objective must ask the pivotal preference or objective question. An infeasible constraint task instead requires Relax : a minimum-cost permitted repair and an action valid under that same repair. These single-source rules do not prioritize simultaneous sources. Formal decision and repair definitions appear in Appendix O . 2.2 Methodology and Experimental Setup Task construction. Each V3 group contains three source-matched action/intervention pairs, yielding six independent tasks. Each pair changes whether intervention is necessary. Preference tasks hide one adjacent comparison, giving two admissible completions. Four structures, three sizes ( n ∈ { 4 , 6 , 8 } n\in\{4,6,8\} ), and three generator seeds form 36 cells; the common evaluation uses 20 complete groups per cell, totaling 4,320 prompts. Exact solvers supply labels, and fixed checkers assess responses without an LLM judge. Local-cue (H5) and output-requirement (H2) comparisons use distinct sampling designs; construction and sampling details are in Appendix M . Models and evaluation procedure. We evaluate GPT-6-Astra ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , Claude-5-Sonnet ( Anthropic, 2026 ) , Gemini-3.1-Pro ( Google DeepMind, 2026 ) , and gpt-oss-120b ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) on V3; the first three also cover H2 and H5. Single-turn requests use fresh conversations without tools or access to private labels; task-completion follow-ups retain their conversation history. Within-model comparisons are primary because inference settings and collection conditions differ. Configuration, record checks, and recovery procedures are documented in Appendix L . Evaluation metrics. Accuracy measures decision-label correctness. Intervention Flip Correctness ( IFC \mathrm{IFC} ) is the fraction of matched pairs with both labels correct, aggregated by pair counts. Fully correct (FC) additionally requires accepted response content; all-six accuracy requires all six labels in a group to be correct. FC measures acceptance under the fixed interface and checker; evidence validity is scored separately (Appendix F ). Unparseable completed responses and unresolved OSS truncations remain unsuccessful, with the latter treated as delivery failures rather than observed reasoning errors (Appendix B.4 ). 3 When Is Intervention Necessary? We examine whether models distinguish a visible source of uncertainty from a necessary intervention, then ask whether their decisions translate into accepted responses and successful task completion. 3.1 Individual Decisions and Matched-Pair Reliability Strong individual decision accuracy coexists with failures to handle both sides of a matched action/intervention contrast. On the common 4,320-prompt V3 subset, GPT-6-Astra achieves 92.57% Accuracy and 85.56% IFC, while all six decisions are correct in 65.00% of groups. These measures distinguish getting an individual response category right from correctly handling every source-matched contrast in a group. Claude-5-Sonnet, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and gpt-oss-120b show the same distinction between individual, pair, and group success; complete results and seed-wise breakdowns are reported in Appendix B . OSS scores retain unresolved truncations in the full denominator, with complete-response results and missing-response bounds reported separately in Appendix B.4 . Astra’s observed IFC is close to its descriptive independence reference of 85.28%, calculated from the action- and intervention-member accuracies within each cell and source (Appendix C ). Matched-pair evaluation measures joint success on both sides of the actionability distinction. Values above bars are percentages. 3.2 Errors Depend on Structure and Source The dominant decision difficulty for Astra and Claude under the original V3 prompts is recognizing when intervention is unnecessary . For Astra, 303 of 321 incorrect or unparseable decisions occur on tasks where action is warranted; for Claude, the corresponding count is 468 of 551 decision errors. Both models correctly identify most constructed intervention-needed cases, yet repeatedly fail to act when the available information already suffices. Success at recognizing the need for clarification or repair therefore does not ensure that a model avoids unnecessary intervention. This asymmetry is accompanied by substantial variation across structures and sources. Across the evaluated configurations, meeting scheduling and apartment choice are handled more reliably than object allocation and stable matching (Figure 2 ). The source profiles are not identical, however: preference pairs have the highest IFC for Astra and Gemini, whereas constraint pairs have the highest IFC for Claude and OSS. Objective pairs are especially difficult for Claude and OSS, and Gemini also makes unnecessary interventions on many objective-source action tasks (Figure 3 ). The source ordering varies across models. OSS uses a distinct inference implementation and budget and retains incomplete responses. Exact values appear in Table 5 ; Gemini collection and scoring details are in Appendix B.2 . 3.3 Correct Labels Do Not Establish Executable Answers Under the original V3 checks, correct decision labels frequently accompany responses that fail the required content checks. This separation appears in all four models (Figure 3 ). For Astra, FC is 50.79%, despite its high decision Accuracy. The clearest example is relaxation: all 720 Relax labels are correct, yet none of the responses passes the complete repair-and-action check. Every response omits or nulls the required top-level action , so no six-task group passes all response-content checks. Some inspected answers place a resulting action in another field, while the original wording does not consistently specify the exact representation required by the checker. This identifies a mismatch between requested and checked content. The other models reinforce the distinction without sharing an identical failure profile. Claude’s rejected responses mix unrecognized field names or action representations with actions outside the accepted set, even though all responses are parseable JSON (Appendix C.1 ). Gemini likewise has many correct decisions whose content is rejected (Appendix B.2 ). For OSS, even the missing-response upper bound on FC remains far below its observed Accuracy, so unresolved truncation alone cannot explain the separation (Appendix B.4 ). The response checks are detailed in Appendix F . Section 5 compares output requirements on the same tasks. 3.4 Task Completion after Intervention A warranted intervention is an intermediate step, not a completed task. Building on evaluation of clarification through the usefulness of its answers ( Rao and Daumë III, 2018 ) , we test whether models can proceed from an accepted intervention to a correct final action. We select 540 intervention-needed tasks by retaining three members from each of five matched groups in every cell. Astra, Claude-5-Sonnet, and Gemini-3.1-Pro use the same tasks and explicit JSON requirements. In this two-step procedure, the first response must specify the intervention and leave action null until feedback. A valid first intervention then receives feedback and a final-action request in the same conversation; an invalid first response receives no second turn. The independent reference route receives predetermined feedback directly (Appendix J ). The results separate failures to initiate the required interaction from failures to solve the updated task. Astra completes 99.07% of tasks autonomously, close to the reference rate of 99.81%; its few failures include both premature actions and incorrect final actions after valid interventions. For Claude, most autonomous failures occur before an accepted intervention has been produced, often because an action is supplied before feedback. Additional failures follow valid interventions, so first-step compliance and final-action correctness must be assessed separately. Detailed rates and recovery accounting, including the two authorized Claude restarts, are reported in Appendix J . Gemini illustrates an even stronger dependence on the response requirements: 501 of 540 first responses wrap JSON in Markdown code fences and are rejected by the fixed bare-JSON parser, preventing feedback and a second turn. Code-fence rejection also affects its autonomous final and reference responses. Completion rates include these parser rejections. The comparison uses intervention-needed tasks; the two routes differ in conversation history and can use different permitted repairs. Appendix J reports first-step validity and final-action success separately. 4 Do Local Cues Explain the Errors? We ask whether the errors observed in Section 3 persist when selected local cues are matched, and whether the answer depends on how the required response is specified. 4.1 Local-Cue-Matched Pairs A source-matched pair can still differ in local features that correlate with its labels. Motivated by documented prompt sensitivity ( Sclar et al., 2023 ; Chatterjee et al., 2024 ) , the H5 collection matches selected source-dependent features while changing whether intervention is necessary. For example, objective pairs preserve the objective menu and per-objective solution counts; allocation-constraint pairs preserve agent and object degrees in permission graphs while differing in whether a complete assignment exists. A deterministic rule using only these identical features cannot distinguish the two members. Solution-count matching is enforced during construction; the solutions remain private. Appendix D details the feature checks and construction differences from V3. We select five of the ten available pairs per source and cell using a fixed seed without consulting model outcomes, yielding 540 pairs and 1,080 logical tasks across all 36 cells. These are two-task pairs, not complete six-task groups. Each task is answered under its original requirements and with appended explicit JSON requirements, identical for both members of a pair. The four requests per pair are randomized and use fresh conversations. Astra’s two conditions are collected within the same run; Claude-5-Sonnet follows the same prompts and order, and a separate Gemini-3.1-Pro replication uses the same fixed subset and four-call design. Each model contributes 2,160 responses. Claude’s quota-related time gaps and Gemini’s recovery batches are documented in Appendix D . 4.2 Matched Cues Do Not Make Errors Format-Invariant Errors remain on locally matched tasks, but their frequency changes markedly with response requirements. For GPT-6-Astra, IFC rises from 76.67% to 98.33% when the required response is made explicit, alongside an increase in individual Accuracy (Figure 4 ). Same-task corrections greatly outnumber reversals. The improvement concerns decision-label correctness, not only whether the accompanying response content passes the FC checks. The aggregate decision improvement replicates in Claude-5-Sonnet and Gemini-3.1-Pro, but its source profile differs. Astra’s largest IFC gain is on preference pairs, while its constraint decisions are already perfect in both conditions. Claude and Gemini benefit most on constraint pairs. Objective pairs remain the least reliable source for Claude under explicit requirements, and Gemini’s objective IFC decreases slightly despite its aggregate gain. Response specification affects decision success across the three models. Strict FC also improves; detailed results are reported in Appendix D , with Gemini’s replication separately documented in Appendix D.1 . Errors persist with matched local features and vary with response requirements. H5 uses a separately constructed task collection, including a different allocation-constraint family. Section 5 compares three output requirements on the same V3 logical instances, measuring decision and response-content correctness separately. 5 How Much Do Output Requirements Matter? We now hold the logical tasks fixed to distinguish improvements in required response content from changes in decision correctness. We also examine whether supplying candidate answers or emphasizing intervention availability produces similar benefits. 5.1 Three Requirements for the Same Tasks Following the distinction between content and format constraints ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) , H2 compares three response requirements on the same 2,160 logical tasks and 1,080 pairs, drawn from ten complete V3 groups per cell. Each task is answered under its original prompt, explicit JSON requirements, and the same JSON requirements plus model-generated evidence. GPT-6-Astra, Claude-5-Sonnet, and Gemini-3.1-Pro each contribute 6,480 responses. The original condition retains any existing request for structured output; it does not mean that JSON was never requested. The explicit condition specifies allowed decision strings, field names, action representations, and source-specific question and correction structures. In particular, a relaxation must include both a permitted change and a valid resulting action in the required top-level field. The evidence condition additionally requests witnesses derived from the public task, such as actions under each preference completion or objective, or an account of infeasibility.
